questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: A field with no net passage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how zero net flux coexists with local passage
questions.stem: In the apiary logbook, explain how a field with zero divergence can still push air through part of a hive entrance, and why the net passage through the closed surface is nevertheless zero.

answer.exemplar: Zero divergence means the field has no sources or sinks, so whatever enters one part of a closed surface must leave through another part. Locally the field can be strong and produce a large flux through a single opening, but the contributions balance over the whole closed surface. The divergence theorem turns the net flux into the integral of the divergence over the enclosed region, and that integral is zero, so the net passage is zero even though individual patches carry real flux.

questions.explanation: Zero divergence removes sources and sinks, so inflow through one part is balanced by outflow through another. Claiming that zero net flux means no local passage confuses a balance with an absence.
questions.hint: Think of the balance between inflow and outflow.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a chart contributes to a surface integral
questions.stem: In the apiary logbook, describe what a surface parametrization carries into the surface integral, and why two charts of one surface can disagree.

answer.exemplar: A parametrization is a map from a region in the plane onto the surface, and it brings along a local measure of stretching, which is the length of the cross product of the two partials. That measure is what the area integral actually uses, so two charts of one surface can report different areas whenever one of them covers the surface more than once or stretches it differently. The surface itself fixes the area; the chart only decides how the integral arrives at it, so the chart must be checked for one-to-one coverage.

questions.explanation: The chart supplies the stretching factor through the cross product of the partials, and a chart covering the surface twice reports twice the area. The surface fixes the true area.
questions.hint: Ask what the cross product of the partials measures.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: The vector area element of a graph
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flux calculation needs a vector area element
questions.stem: Explain in the apiary logbook why the vector area element of a graph is needed for a flux calculation, and what it contributes that a scalar area element does not.

answer.exemplar: The scalar area element dS tells us only how much surface a patch covers, which is enough for a mass integral. The vector area element carries a direction: it is perpendicular to the surface and its length is the stretching factor of the map. When it is dotted with the field, the scalar product selects exactly the component of the field that crosses the surface, so orientation and angle are both built in. That is why flux integrals need the vector form and mass integrals do not.

questions.explanation: The vector element is perpendicular to the surface and scaled by the local stretch, so its dot product with the field isolates the crossing component. A scalar element ignores orientation.
questions.hint: Ask what a dot product with the field selects.

options.misconception: treats a parametrization as a shape with no extra data

options.text: It carries the mass of the surface, so a mass integral needs no density at all.
options.misconception: believes a parametrization supplies physical density

options.text: It carries nothing extra, since the same surface may be described in many ways.
options.misconception: claims all parametrizations carry identical data

questions.explanation: A parametrization is a map from a parameter region onto the surface, and the map carries a stretching factor and an orientation, so different charts of one surface can give different numbers.
questions.hint: Think about the cross product of the partials.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: The vector area element of a graph
questions.learningObjective: Compute a flux from tabulated projected areas and field components
questions.stem: The apiary logbook tabulates two panels of a hive cover: panel one has projected area 6 square decimetres with upward field component 3, and panel two has projected area 4 square decimetres with component 5. What is the flux through the two panels of the cover?

options.text: The total flux is 32, which is the sum of the two upward components times the total area.
options.misconception: multiplies the summed components by the summed area

options.text: The total flux is 38, obtained by adding 6 times 3 and 4 times 5.
The total flux is 8, because the upward components add directly over the cover.
options.misconception: adds the components without the projected areas

options.text: The total flux is 20, because the larger projected area contributes nothing to the flux.
options.misconception: ignores one of the two panels entirely

questions.explanation: Flux on a panel is the upward component times the projected area, so 18 and 20 give 38. Adding the components 3 and 5 forgets that each acts over its own area.
questions.hint: Weight each upward component by its projected area.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compare the flux through two plates tilted at different angles
questions.stem: Two flat hive lids of 0.4 square metres each are tilted at 30 and 60 degrees from the horizontal in the same vertical field of strength 3. Which lid carries more flux and by how much?

options.text: The lid at 30 degrees carries less, because a flatter lid presents more area to the field.
options.misconception: thinks flatter means less flux, ignoring the projection

options.text: Both lids carry the same flux, because they have equal area and the field is the same.
options.misconception: ignores the tilt when comparing the two lids

options.text: The 30 degree lid carries 1.04 against 0.6, so it carries about 1.73 times as much.
Neither flux can be found, because the field would have to be measured on each lid.
options.misconception: demands a field value that is already given

questions.explanation: The 30 degree lid gives 3 times 0.4 times the cosine of 30 degrees, about 1.04, and the 60 degree lid gives 0.6, and the ratio is 1.73. Equal areas do not equalize flux.
questions.hint: Insert the cosine of each lid's tilt angle.
